title: An intra-host mathematical model for rabies infection with structured axonal transport and post-exposure control strategies

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to develop a mathematical model that captures the complex dynamics of rabies virus infection within a host, addressing the need for a more detailed understanding of viral progression and post-exposure control strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study presents a mathematical model of rabies virus infection, focusing on the intra-host dynamics of the virus from the inoculation site to the salivary glands, and includes three time-dependent post-exposure control strategies.
analysis.methods: The model is formulated as a system of nonlinear ordinary differential equations, incorporating structured retrograde axonal transport, local effector immune response, and three time-dependent post-exposure control strategies. An optimal control problem is formulated to minimize viral load and salivary dissemination under intervention cost constraints.
analysis.main_results: Mathematical analysis confirms the positivity and boundedness of solutions, establishes the existence and uniqueness of a global solution, identifies a disease-free equilibrium, and derives a basic reproduction number R0 defining a threshold for local infection establishment.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the model as a rigorous basis for evaluating post-exposure prophylactic strategies, with a key novelty being the explicit representation of neurotropic progression via discrete axonal steps.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide a framework for understanding the dynamics of rabies virus infection and for developing optimized post-exposure interventions, which can inform surveillance and control strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a mathematical model and does not include empirical data, which may affect the strength of the evidence. The evidence is considered moderate as it is based on theoretical analysis and simulations.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a novel intra-host mathematical model for rabies virus infection, integrating the stages of viral progression from the inoculation site to the salivary glands. The model incorporates structured retrograde axonal transport, local immune response, and three post-exposure control strategies. Mathematical analysis confirms the model's positivity, boundedness, and existence of a global solution, identifying a disease-free equilibrium and a basic reproduction number R0. The model offers a framework for studying therapeutic windows and optimizing interventions, with implications for surveillance and control strategies. However, the study is limited to theoretical analysis and simulations, which may affect the strength of the evidence. The findings are considered moderate in evidence strength as they are based on mathematical modeling rather than empirical data.

title: Atypical Rabies Encephalomyelitis Following Incomplete Post-Exposure Prophylaxis: Delayed Serological Diagnosis and Survival in an Adolescent.

analysis.methods: Initial rabies reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) antibody testing were negative. Serial evaluation subsequently demonstrated rising rabies virus-neutralizing antibody titers in both serum and CSF, confirming rabies encephalitis.
analysis.main_results: With intensive supportive care, the patient survived the acute illness but was discharged with persistent neurological deficits.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of atypical rabies and underscores the importance of complete post-exposure prophylaxis.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Although he completed post-exposure rabies vaccination, rabies immunoglobulin was not administered.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations or evidence strength for the study.

title: Comparing NGO and government-managed dog vaccination: Implications for vaccination coverage and rabies outcomes in animals and humans in Meru, Tanzania

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rabies is a fatal but preventable zoonotic disease transmitted primarily by domestic dogs. Mass dog vaccination (MDV) is central to rabies elimination, yet vaccination coverage in endemic settings often remains insufficient and uneven.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study assessed dog vaccination coverage under two contrasting delivery arrangements in Meru, Tanzania: Organised, non-government (NGO)-managed annual MDV campaigns and predominantly owner-initiated vaccination services in government-managed wards. Vaccination coverage in both NGO and government-managed wards was estimated using household surveys conducted after NGO-managed campaigns and in government-managed wards where no organised annual MDV campaigns were implemented.
analysis.methods: Vaccination data from NGO-managed MDV campaigns (2020–2024) were obtained from Mbwa wa Africa records, and 2025 data were collected during campaign implementation. Data on human exposures and suspected animal cases (2023–2025) were extracted from the Integrated Bite Case Management System. Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were used to compare vaccination coverage between the two settings and to assess the association among vaccination coverage, human exposures, and animal cases.
analysis.main_results: Vaccination coverage in NGO-managed wards increased from 45.1% in 2020 to 71% in 2025, while government-managed wards remained low, peaking at 21.9% in 2023 before declining to 8.8% in 2025. Human exposures and animal cases declined in 2024 but increased in 2025. Animal rabies cases were associated with human exposures. Vaccination coverage was not associated with human exposures (IRR = 1.0, 95% CI: 0.998–1.010, p = 0.730) but was associated with animal cases (IRR = 1.02, 95% CI: 1.01–1.04, p = 0.008).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: GLMM analysis confirmed higher vaccination coverage in NGO-managed wards (IRR = 12.1, 95% CI: 12.1–12.2; p < 0.05). The findings highlight the importance of accessible, coordinated, and equitable dog vaccination services integrated with One Health surveillance.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide evidence that coordinated, cross-sectoral planning – linking veterinary vaccination campaigns, human health surveillance, and community engagement – is essential to achieve and sustain elimination targets. By integrating mass dog vaccination data with Integrated Bite Case Management (IBCM) surveillance data, we show how disparities in animal health service delivery directly translate into human rabies exposure risk.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations in the study design. The evidence strength is high as the study provides detailed statistical analysis and uses multiple data sources.

analysis.summary_en: This study compares NGO and government-managed dog vaccination programs in Meru, Tanzania, to assess their impact on rabies coverage and outcomes. Rabies, a fatal zoonotic disease, is primarily transmitted by domestic dogs, and mass dog vaccination is crucial for elimination. The research highlights that NGO-managed campaigns achieved significantly higher vaccination coverage than government-managed wards, with coverage increasing from 45.1% to 71% in NGO areas between 2020 and 2025. The findings emphasize the need for coordinated, cross-sectoral planning and equitable service delivery to achieve rabies elimination goals. title: RVG29-modified reduction-responsive nanomicelles for brain-targeted delivery of a glutaminyl cyclase inhibitor in Alzheimer's disease.

analysis.methods: The platform was functionalized with RVG29 to enhance brain delivery and release of the active thiol form of B13, an imidazole-based QC inhibitor, through a disulfide linker.
analysis.main_results: RVG29 modification increased cellular uptake in bEND.3, PC12, and SH-SY5Y cells, enhanced transport across a bEND.3 monolayer by 3.12-fold, and elevated brain fluorescence accumulation in vivo by 2.58-fold and 1.96-fold compared with free Cy5 and unmodified micelles, respectively.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a novel nanomicellar delivery system for brain-targeted administration of a glutaminyl cyclase inhibitor in Alzheimer's disease. In 8-month-old 3 × Tg-AD mice, the administration of RVG29-PIC-B13 led to improved performance in several behavioral assays, indicating potential therapeutic benefits. Mechanistically, the system inhibited brain glutaminyl cyclase activity, reduced Aβ and pE-Aβ burden, and preserved dendritic complexity and spine density. Preliminary biocompatibility analyses were favorable, but the study's limitations include reliance on animal models and the absence of long-term safety data. These findings support RVG29-PIC-B13 as a promising strategy for enhancing the therapeutic outcomes of glutaminyl cyclase inhibitors in Alzheimer's disease.

The study found that all sixteen pinnipeds seroconverted and remained seropositive, with antibody titers above the 0.5 IU/L threshold. The authors concluded that the vaccine was safe and provided protective immunity for about three years, recommending booster doses. The findings suggest that triannual vaccination could be a useful strategy for controlling rabies in pinniped populations. However, the study's reliance on historical serum samples limits the confidence in its conclusions, and the evidence strength is moderate.

title: Histopathology results of vaccination sites collected from New Zealand white rabbits vaccinated with a lanolin-based Rabisin® vaccine

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess whether a slow-release water in-oil emulsion rabies vaccine could potentially provide a safe and effective method to improve canine rabies control in future.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We evaluated the safety and efficacy of a single dose of a lanolin-based adjuvant combined with a commercially available rabies vaccine used in canines (Rabisin®), compared to two doses of Rabisin® in 16 New Zealand white rabbits.
analysis.methods: Histopathology evaluation of the injection sites revealed only mild microscopic signs of inflammation, no abscessation or granuloma formation in either the lanolin or Rabisin® groups.
analysis.main_results: Six of the eight samples collected from the Rabisin® group demonstrated a mild inflammatory infiltrate composed predominantly of eosinophils with fewer lymphocytes and scant plasma cells, whereas the remaining two samples showed minimal to no inflammatory changes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The biopsy sample collected on day 89 of the study from a female in the Rabisin® group was found to be within normal limits (no microscopic lesions), while one sample (from male number 21) had a single focus of locally extensive fibrous connective tissue with scant eosinophils and a few lymphocytes and plasma cells within the superficial dermis.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the lanolin-based adjuvant may be a viable alternative to traditional rabies vaccine formulations in terms of minimizing local inflammatory responses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its small sample size and use of rabbits as a model, which may not fully represent canine immune responses. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the safety and efficacy of a lanolin-based adjuvant combined with a commercially available rabies vaccine (Rabisin®) in New Zealand white rabbits, comparing it to two doses of Rabisin®. Histopathology of injection sites showed mild inflammation in most samples from the Rabisin® group, with some exhibiting minimal to no changes. The lanolin group had similar findings but with fewer inflammatory cells in one sample. These results suggest that the lanolin-based adjuvant may offer a safer alternative for rabies vaccination, though the small sample size and use of rabbits as a model limit the strength of the evidence. The study contributes to understanding vaccine safety in animal models, which could inform future canine rabies control strategies.
